entries.title: Trump says AI companies agree to 'self-police'
entries.summary: Donald Trump said the US won't "stifle" the development of AI, which he sees as "bigger than the Industrial Revolution." The agreement comes amid mounting concerns over AI safety after recent hacking incidents.
entries.content:
United States of America

Trump says AI companies agree to 'self-police'

September 30, 2026

Donald Trump said the US won't "stifle" the development of AI, which he sees as "bigger than the Industrial Revolution." The agreement comes amid mounting concerns over AI safety after recent hacking incidents.

US President Donald Trump on Tuesday said a group of CEOs of Artificial Intelligence (AI) companies had signed an accord to "self-police" the technology's development.

Trump met with AI leaders at the White House, where he doubled down on his support for the technology.

The agreement comes as public scrutiny has grown over the risks posed by the emerging technology, following reports that OpenAI and Anthropic's AI agents had gone rogue and hacked into other companies' systems.

Concerns are also mounting over the industry's growing footprint in communities, particularly with the growth of data centers.

Prior to the meeting, Trump had reiterated that his government would not limit the development of AI or support calls for "guardrails" or other restrictions on the sector.

"I will never stifle the growth of a technology that will be bigger than the Industrial Revolution," Trump said. "We can't stifle it, and we're leading by a lot."

Trump also announced that he would officially rename the technology "super intelligence" because "it's not artificial."

Which AI leaders were at the White House meeting?

House Speaker Mike Johnson joined the meeting, which included top AI executives like Anthropic's Dario Amodei, OpenAI president Greg Brockman, Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, and Elon Musk, whose X social media platform includes its own AI model, Grok.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella also attended.

"I think I'm seeing tremendous self-policing. And they understand that they have to self-police," Trump told reporters during an impromptu press conference outside the West Wing.

Later, the US president posted a copy of the "White House Accord on Super Intelligence" on his Truth Social platform.

What does the AI accord say?

"Every company is responsible for developing its own technology safely and in a way that builds trust with customers and the public," the accord begins.

The document affirms that tech companies will implement "robust internal controls to ensure all of the controls, monitoring, and detection are operating as intended, and that any issues are remediated."

They are to "empower an internal team" to ensure "control, monitoring, and detection" are working as intended.

AI companies are also expected to "partner with an independent external auditor or evaluator to carry out independent assessments," as well as "designate an independent committee of the board of directors" to oversee and receive reports.

Trump said the agreement is "morally binding" but not legally enforceable.

The accord does, however, leave the door open "to codify these steps into laws or regulations."

Edited by: Karl Sexton

entries.title: Morocco: King appoints first woman prime minister
entries.summary: The appointment of Fatima Zahra Mansouri comes after her center-right party won last week's parliamentary elections in Morocco. She had previously served as mayor of the city of Marrakesh.
entries.content:
Morocco

Morocco: King appoints first woman prime minister

September 29, 2026

The appointment of Fatima Zahra Mansouri comes after her center-right party won last week's parliamentary elections in Morocco. She had previously served as mayor of the city of Marrakesh.

Fatima Zahra Mansouri became Morocco's first female prime minister, the country's royal cabinet announced on Tuesday. King Mohammed VI has tasked her with forming the next government.

Under the Moroccan constitution, the country's king has the power to appoint the prime minister, but he must choose someone from the party that wins the most seats in parliamentary elections.

Mansouri's appointment comes after her center-right Authenticity and Modernity Party (PAM) won last week's parliamentary elections.

PAM raked in 97 out of 395 seats in the House of Representatives, 31 more than the next closest competitor. The vote was, however, marred by the lowest turnout in two decades.

"For the first time in our country's history, a woman is taking on the responsibility of leading the government," Mansouri said. "This is a source of pride not only for me but for all Moroccan women."

Mansouri is now the second woman in the Arab world to serve as prime minister, after Najla Bouden, who served in that position in Tunisia from 2021 to 2023.

First female mayor of Marrakesh

Mansouri's government will now need to deliver on voter's most important issues, such as fighting inflation, raising wages and creating jobs. At the same time, she is expected to oversee billions of dollars in investments linked to Morocco co-hosting the 2030 FIFA World Cup during her tenure.

"We are fully aware that this period will be significant and marked by high expectations from Moroccans, particularly young people," Mansouri said. "That is why we will have a program offering concrete and realistic solutions to citizens' concerns," she added.

Mansouri was the first woman to serve as mayor of Marrakesh. She was elected mayor in 2009 and served for six years. She retook the job again in 2021. In addition to her mayorship, she has also been a member of parliament.

The 50-year-old has been a member of PAM since 2008, the year the party was founded by current royal adviser Fouad Ali El Himma. PAM was formed to serve as a counterweight to the country's Islamist movement.

By 2024, Mansouri was one of the party's top leaders.

Her task now will be to form a government and for that, PAM has expressed willingness to work with all parties. Some, however, including the moderate Islamist Justice and Development party and left-wing Federation of Democratic Left, have said they plan to remain in the opposition.

Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko

entries.title: Estonia blames Russia for arson attack on defense company
entries.summary: The Estonian government accused Moscow of an "act of sabotage" that is part of Russia's broader campaign across Europe. The Baltic state has received support from EU and NATO leaders.
entries.content:
Europe

Estonia blames Russia for arson attack on defense company

September 29, 2026

The Estonian government accused Moscow of an "act of sabotage" that is part of Russia's broader campaign across Europe. The Baltic state has received support from EU and NATO leaders.

NATO and EU leaders rallied behind Estonia on Tuesday, after the Baltic country accused Russia of being behind an arson attack in its capital Tallinn.

Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said Moscow was found responsible for the August 15 arson attack against defense company Milrem Robotics, after the government conducted an investigation into the incident.

Milrem Robotics develops ground drones that are used in Ukraine.

"We can conclude with certainty that the arson attack... was an act of sabotage ordered by the special services of the Russian Federation," Tsahkna said on X, adding that the perpetrators had been arrested, and Russia's ambassador had been summoned.

"This act of sabotage is part of Russia's broader campaign across Europe, aimed at intimidating us and weakening our support for Ukraine," Tsahkna said.

NATO chief Mark Rutte backed Estonia, accusing Russia of furthering "its reckless campaign of hostile actions against NATO allies."

Rutte also said Russia was "failing on the battlefield in Ukraine " while also failing to undermine NATO's unity.

Kremlin says links to arson are "baseless"

Estonia, an EU and NATO member, has a population of 1.3 million and borders Russia to the east. 

The incident took place on the night of August 15, when a fire broke out in a building used by Milrem Robotics in Tallinn. According to a statement from the Estonian government, authorities were on the scene right away and no injuries were reported.

Three suspects were later detained in Latvia in connection with the arson attack and were handed over to Estonia this month.

The Kremlin responded to the arson investigation findings by dismissing them as "baseless" and with "absolutely no relation to reality."

"We cannot and will not take such statements seriously," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters in Moscow.

EU and NATO leaders rally behind Estonia

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul pledged Germany's "full solidarity" with Estonia. "Russia's reckless hostilities will not divide us. They only strengthen our resolve to bolster NATO deterrence and support Ukraine," Wadephul wrote on X.

The EU said it stood by Estonia, saying the arson attack was "reckless" and would not deter the bloc in its support for Ukraine.

"Moscow is trying to scare Europe into winding down its support for Ukraine. This will not happen," European Commission spokesman Christian Wigand said.

French President Emmanuel Macron labeled the attack a "dangerous escalation" by Russia. He said it represented another in a "multiplication of these hostile acts."

"Russia needs to know that it will not overcome our unity or our determination to continue supporting Ukraine," Macron wrote on X.

Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kestutis Budrys said "Russia's fingerprints are all over" the arson attack, adding that it was proof that Moscow's "hostile activities do not stop at Ukraine's borders."

Neighboring Latvia's President Edgars Rinkevics said in response to the incident that "more support for Ukraine... will be needed and must be provided."

Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson also commented ont he matter, saying attribution of the arson attack was "extremely serious" and "directed against Europe as a whole."

Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko

entries.title: Germany news: Bremerhaven port to receive defense boost
entries.summary: Bremerhaven's port and Bremen's airport will be upgraded for German, NATO defense needs in case of an attack on the alliance. It comes as European countries upgrade militarily amid Russia's war in Ukraine. DW has more.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Bremerhaven port to receive defense boost

Published September 29, 2026last updated September 30, 2026

Bremerhaven's port and Bremen's airport will be upgraded for German, NATO defense needs in case of an attack on the alliance. It comes as European countries upgrade militarily amid Russia's war in Ukraine. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

This blog has closed. Below is a roundup of the main headlines in Germany on Tuesday, September 29, 2026:

  • Bremerhaven's port to be upgraded for German, NATO defense needs
  • Police cars in Rhineland-Palatinate to be equipped with teddy bears
  • Historic German brewery to close after nearly 400 years
  • Friedrich Merz and five others threaten to block EU budget proposal
  • EU budget proposal slated to be approved by end of year by all 27 EU states
  • Merz says Russia 'not interested' in serious talks after Wadephul-Lavrov meeting 
  • Coalition talks are underway in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania

If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your preferred source on Google, so you'll always see our verified news first.

Skip next section Thousands evacuated over US-made WWII bomb in Cologne

Thousands evacuated over US-made WWII bomb in Cologne

Around 3,000 people were ordered to evacuate their homes in Cologne after the authorities discovered a World War II-era bomb near the Rhine river.

Authorities said the 1-ton bomb was discovered due to the river's  low water levels. In parallel with the evacuation order, authorities temporarily closed the Rhine to traffic and blocked a nearby motorway, or Autobahn, as they are known in Germany.

Three people were fined during the evacuation effort — two for refusing to leave their apartments and one for entering the secure zone.

The disposal team was unable to remove the detonator at the scene, prompting authorities to transport the ordinance to a different location. Once in an open field, the bomb was placed in a hole and covered with 60 tons of sand, with the bomb disposal unit then conducting a controlled detonation.

Unexploded bombs are still being discovered across Germany over eight decades since the end of World War II, often prompting mass evacuations.

Skip next section UK Oscar winner Helen Mirren honored in Hamburg

UK Oscar winner Helen Mirren honored in Hamburg

Movie star Helen Mirren received the Douglas Sirk Award at Germany's FilmFest Hamburg.

The veteran actress, now 81 years old, said she was honored to be awarded for her body of work.

"I've worked consistently all through my life, there has never been literally one year... that I haven't worked, so it is quite nice to have a recognition for that," she told reporters.

"So I will be proud."

The annual FilmFest Hamburg is one of Germany's top movie festivals.

The Douglas Sirk Award is a non-monetary prize given to people who contributed to the film industry and culture.

It is named after Hamburg-born US director Douglas Sirk, who died in 1987.

Skip next section Hanover-Berlin train line to be closed for 14 months

Hanover-Berlin train line to be closed for 14 months

The train line between the major German cities of Hanover and Berlin is expected to be closed for 14 months starting from Friday due to renovations.

Instrastructure and tracks will be replaced on a stretch with a total length of 227 kilometers (141 miles) until December 2027.

According to Germany's rail service Deutsche Bahn, trains will be redirected via Braunschweig and Magdeburg and will take around 80 minutes longer to travel.

High-speed Intercity Express trains between Berlin and the western state of North Rhine-Westphalia will also be impacted, along with regional trains.

Skip next section Merz on Wadephul-Lavrov meeting: Russia 'not interested' in serious talks

Merz on Wadephul-Lavrov meeting: Russia 'not interested' in serious talks

During a press conference in Berlin, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the meeting between German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul and his counterpart Sergey Lavrov showed Russia is "not interested" in serious talks to end the war in Ukraine.  

The Wadephul-Lavrov meeting was the first time the German and Russian sides met in person since the beginning of the Russian full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

"Russia's subsequent assessment of this conversation has shown that Russia is obviously not interested in serious talks at all at this point in time," Merz said.

During a speech at the UN General Assembly debate following the meeting with Wadephul, Lavrov said the "aims of the special military operation will be achieved," referring to Russia's official term for the war.

Merz urged the Russian government to come to the negotiating table.

"But if Russia is not prepared to do so, then we are... ready to support Ukraine over a long period of time," Merz said. The German chancellor said "Russia will not win this war" and pointed at the "precarious situation" of the Russian economy.

Skip next section Bremerhaven's port to be upgraded for German, NATO defense needs

Bremerhaven's port to be upgraded for German, NATO defense needs

The North Sea port of Bremerhaven will be upgraded to better serve German and NATO defense needs, German officials said on Tuesday.

German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius signed a memorandum of understanding on Tuesday which will transform the port into a "Deployment Hub" in the case of an attack on the NATO bloc. The plan will cost some €1.5 billion ($1.7 billion).

Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022 has caused European countries to draw up plans in case of an attack on a NATO member, such as Germany. 

"Tens of thousands of soldiers will need accomodation and food. Machinery and equipment must be maintained and operated accordingly," Pistorius said.

Bridges, roads and railways will need to be boosted to facilitate the transportation of NATO equipment arriving at the Bremerhaven port. Bremen's airport will also be expanded with more logistics space as part of the plan.   

Skip next section Police cars in Rhineland-Palatinate to be equipped with teddy bears

Police cars in Rhineland-Palatinate to be equipped with teddy bears

Police cars in the western German state of Rhineland-Palatinate will soon come equipped with a new cute and cuddly weapon ― teddy bears. 

The state's interior minister, Achim Schweikert of the center-right Christian Democratic Union, said the bears will be given to kids by officers as a "source of comfort" in emergency situations. So far, 1,100 bears have been bought by police, equating to three bears per car.

It's up to police to decide when to give out the bears to children.

The decision to equip the police with teddy bears is due to a bachelor thesis at the Rhineland-Pfalz Police Academy by Kim and Kevin Zorn. The couple are both police officers in the major city of Koblenz.

The thesis researched the first aid provided to children in emergency situations. Children who witness situations such as domestic violence or sexual abuse can be distracted if they have an object hold on to.

Teddy bears are already being used by police in other German states, such as Saxony-Anhalt.

Skip next section SPD leaders call for review of possible AfD ban

SPD leaders call for review of possible AfD ban

Parliamentary leaders from the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) have called for a formal review of whether Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) should be banned.

"Democracy is threatened by it from within," SPD leaders from the federal parliament, Germany's states and the European Parliament said in a joint declaration after meeting in Bremen.

The resolution described the AfD as a right-wing extremist party that systematically attacks Germany's free society, normalizes racism and seeks to undermine the democratic order from within.

The SPD leaders called for a joint federal-state working group to be established before the end of the year to prepare the review.

"Preparing an examination procedure is a legal necessity required by the protection of our constitution," they said. "We see this as our democratic duty."

Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said such a review was important because every liberal democracy was vulnerable and could also be destroyed from within.

Skip next section Western Germans inherit four times as much as easterners

Western Germans inherit four times as much as easterners

West Germans received more than four times as much inherited or gifted wealth per person as people in the east in 2025, highlighting the country's persistent wealth divide.

More than €2,100 ($2,390) per person was passed down or gifted in western Germany, compared with just under €500 in the eastern states and Berlin, the Federal Statistical Office said. The national average was just over €1,800.

Although the east and Berlin were home to 19% of Germany's population, they accounted for only 5% of the inheritances and gifts assessed for tax.

Tax authorities recorded transfers worth €142.5 billion in western Germany, dwarfing the €8 billion recorded in the east and Berlin.

The divide was also reflected in the tax assessed. Western states accounted for €20.4 billion, or 95%, of Germany's €21.4 billion in inheritance and gift taxes.

Eastern states and Berlin accounted for just €1 billion. The revenue goes directly to Germany's federal states.

Skip next section Historic German brewery to close after nearly 400 years

Historic German brewery to close after nearly 400 years

Wolters brewery in the northern German city of Braunschweig is to stop producing beer at the end of the year, bringing almost four centuries of brewing at the site to an end.

The closure will affect around 90 employees, who have been informed of the decision, according to the law firm handling the company's insolvency proceedings.

Founded in 1627, Wolters filed for insolvency under self-administration in the summer, citing falling sales in Germany's shrinking beer market. Efforts to find an investor for the production site were unsuccessful.

Germany's beer market contracted more sharply in 2025 than in any year since reunification, according to the Federal Statistical Office.

The Food, Beverages and Catering Union criticized the speed of the closure decision, saying the process appeared less like an orderly restructuring and more like "slamming on the brakes."

The Wolters brand could still survive. The insolvency law firm said talks with several interested parties were continuing, although they would not necessarily keep production in Braunschweig.

"An era is coming to an end with the closure of the Braunschweig production site," managing director Nils Handke said, describing the decision as unavoidable.

Skip next section Germany warns Slovakia against doubting NATO defense

Germany warns Slovakia against doubting NATO defense

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has indirectly criticized Slovakia's stance on Russia's war in Ukraine, warning that doubts about NATO deterrence could endanger the entire alliance.

"The greatest threat to freedom on our continent comes from Moscow. The greatest danger to Europe is Putin's belligerent imperialism," Wadephul said during talks with Slovak Foreign Minister Juraj Blanar in Bratislava.

"Questioning these facts is not only lacking in solidarity, it would be irresponsible," he added. Wadephul said countries that doubted NATO's deterrence created risks for themselves and weakened security guarantees for all allies.

Slovakia's left-nationalist Prime Minister Robert Fico has increasingly accused Western countries of escalating tensions with Moscow and questioned the policies of both NATO and the European Union.

Fico recently said he would prefer Slovakia to be neutral and expressed doubt that NATO allies would send troops to defend the country in an emergency. However, he acknowledged that Slovakia remained bound by its NATO membership.

Skip next section Merz calls teachers Germany's most important profession

Merz calls teachers Germany's most important profession

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has praised teachers as "the most important professional group in our country" at the German School Award ceremony in Berlin.

"I speak as a father and grandfather: We entrust you with the most valuable thing we have. Our children," Merz said.

Against the backdrop of Germany's weak results in the PISA international education assessment, Merz said ensuring that young people receive a good education was "one of the most important, if not the most important, tasks facing our society."

The chancellor admitted that he "rarely felt like" going to school as a child but said the ceremony had encouraged him to visit schools more frequently.

The €100,000 ($114,000) top prize went to the Bertha von Suttner Comprehensive School in the central state of Hesse, for its data-driven teaching model and personal support for pupils.

The jury said dedicated departments at the school evaluate data and use the findings to improve lessons. Students also have designated staff members who serve as permanent points of contact.

Only 15% of pupils arrive with a recommendation to attend a gymnasium, Germany's academically oriented secondary school. However, two-thirds later obtain the Abitur qualification needed to enter university, according to the jury.

Skip next section Ukrainian defense minister cancels trip to Germany amid intensifying Russian strikes

Ukrainian defense minister cancels trip to Germany amid intensifying Russian strikes

Ukrainian defense minister has canceled his trip to Germany on Tuesday as Russia hammers the country withround-the-clock drone attacks to wear down its capital and the economy.

Yevgeniy Khmara was scheduled to meet his German counterpart Boris Pistorius at a time when Ukraine has been pushing for allies to step up military and financial aid ahead of winter.

At least nine people were killed across the country on Monday when Moscow's forces pounded apartment buildings, offices as well as a building of the National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine in downtown Kyiv.

The AFP news agency cited an unnamed source telling it that Khmara had canceled trips to both Germany and Norway "due to the situation in Ukraine and intensification of Russian attacks, which requires rapid attention."

Skip next section Patricia Schlesinger: Ex-RBB director's trial date set for November 10

Patricia Schlesinger: Ex-RBB director's trial date set for November 10

The former director of Berlin-based broadcaster RBB (Rundfunk Berlin-Brandenburg) is to stand trial in connection with allegations of financial mismanagement and misuse of company resources that emerged when she was heading the channel in 2022.

The public prosecutor's office filed criminal charges against Patricia Schlesinger and three others last year in December.

The Berlin regional court on Tuesday accepted that indictment, meaning that it believes the case has enough weight to move to trial.

The trial, which is scheduled to begin on November 10, is set to see 56 hearing days because the trial is likely going to be a complex one.

The case is a very high-profile one because it involves someone who was at the helm of Germany's public broadcasting system as Schlesinger was also the director of ARD, the powerful association of the country's nine regional stations.

Schlesinger has denied all allegations. "Ms. Schlesinger based all her decisions as director solely on the interests of RBB. We will fully refute the accusations," her lawyer Oliver Sahan told German press agency DPA.

The trial ends at the end of June 2027, a spokesperson for the Berlin court told reporters.

Skip next section Germany intends to block sale of Hamburg logistics firm to China's Cosco

Germany intends to block sale of Hamburg logistics firm to China's Cosco

The German government intends to block the sale of logistics firm Zippel to Chinese state-owned group Cosco over security risks, the Handelsblatt newspaper reported.

The newspaper cited a restricted government memo that mentioned security and strategic risks that could come with the planned deal.

Cosco, which is one of the world's largest container shipping companies, last year announced that it would like to acquire an 80% stake in Zippel. It already has a minority stake in Hamburg's port terminal.

Zippel, a traditional German company based in Hamburg, the country's largest port city, arranges transportation of freight and cargo.

A number of ministries have been in favor of blocking the deal.

A final decision has yet to be made.

Skip next section CDU struggles: A trip to Sardinia and a beach chair at the chancellery

CDU struggles: A trip to Sardinia and a beach chair at the chancellery

The center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) led by Chancellor Friedrich Merz's party has seen better days: Most recently, it suffered unprecedented defeats in state elections in Saxony-Anhalt, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, and Berlin. At this time of voter disenchantment, two prominent CDU politicians have come under fire on social media: Jens Spahn and Philipp Amthor have been facing accusation of being out of touch and self-absorbed.

A few weeks ago, Spahn resigned from his powerful position as parliamentary group leader of the CDU and CSU bloc in the Bundestag after Spahn had announced that had become a parent with the help of a surrogate mother in the United States. He was accused of hypocrisy because surrogacy is banned in Germany and the CDU and Spahn himself had repeatedly voted to uphold this ban.

Spahn was then given a seat on the influential Budget Committee. He called in sick for a meeting, but at the same time the tabloid BILD published a photograph of him vacationing in Sardinia with his young son. Spahn immediately resigned that post as well.

The CDU's Philipp Amthor has only recently become Minister of State for Federal-State Cooperation in the Chancellor’s Office. There, he placed a beach chair on the balcony of his new office and proudly showed it to a TV reporter. As a reminder: His party has just been voted out of the state parliament in his home state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania on the Baltic Sea coast. But that didn't seem to have dampened the minister's good spirits.

Once again, social media reactions were fierce: This time with criticism of the young government official’s alleged arrogance. Amthor swiftly had the beach chair removed.

As the German saying goes, "Wer den Schaden hat, braucht für den Spott nicht zu Sorgen" (He who suffers the loss need not worry about the ridicule). That is seen to apply quite accurately to the CDU at the moment.

entries.title: Ethiopia: No regard for civilians as fighting in Ethiopia's Tigray region continues
entries.summary: Fighting has returned to northern Ethiopia, shattering a fragile peace in the region. DW spoke to civilians caught in the crossfire amid communication blackouts, as rebel and federal forces keep battling for territory.
entries.content:
Ethiopia

No regard for civilians as fighting in Ethiopia continues

September 29, 2026

Fighting has returned to northern Ethiopia, shattering a fragile peace in the region. DW spoke to civilians caught in the crossfire amid communication blackouts, as rebel and federal forces keep battling for territory.

As fighting keeps spreading across northern Ethiopia, civilians find themselves caught in the crossfire between opposing forces. Little information is emerging from the affected area as the internet and other communication services remain largely disrupted.

However, DW managed to speak to eyewitnesses whose accounts point to a growing toll on civilians.

A 22-year-old woman from the small town of Selenwuha told DW that her relatives were sheltering at home when heavy weaponry shelling struck their residences.

"I have lost six family members," she said. "Those who survived the attack, including the wounded, are currently confined to their homes.

"They have no access to medical facilities or vehicles, and the nearest treatment center is far away."

Strategic town of Alamata reported taken by ENDF

According to local residents, several violent incidents took place in recent days, especially in the border region between the Tigray and Amhara regions, with multiple further reports of civilians being killed by artillery fire.

The overall strategic situation on the ground meanwhile remains difficult to assess, with both rebel and federal forces reportedly making advances in different areas.

DW heard from a source in Tigray that the Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF) keeps advancing towards the regional capital Mekelle. The ENDDF is the country's official military force.

Tigrayan forces are reportedly fighting to defend other towns, including Mekoni and Maychew in southern Tigray, the source told DW on the strict condition of anonymity.

Pro-government militia and affiliated media outlets in the country had reported earlier that the ENDF had made significant progress by seizing control of Alamata in southern Tigray on September 27.

The purported takeover was also recorded by the US-based conflict-monitoring organization ACLED (Armed Conflict Location & Event Data).

Located about 120 kilometers south of the regional capital Mekelle, the strategically important town is situated on a major highway.

During the 2020-2022 war, Alamata changed hands several times between the two warring parties.

Residents accuse federal forces of deliberate attacks

A 40-year-old resident of Alamata told DW that civilians had deliberately been targeted, citing the account shared by militia members in the region.

"The attacks… were acts of retaliation against the people of Alamata," the local said. "The militias told us that government forces had fired the artillery at us."

Another resident, aged 45, said he believed the attack had deliberately been timed to maximize civilian casualties during the opening hours of a market, "when large numbers of people would be gathered there."

"At the Saturday market in Alamata, 11 people were killed and 15 others were wounded", he told DW.

It's important to note that these claims could not be independently verified.

An ENDF spokesperson was also contacted by DW for comment; by the time of the publishing of this article, the spokesperson had not responded to the request.

Shifting alliances and mutual blame

Large-scale fighting erupted on September 23, when Tigrayan forces seized the airports of the regional capital Mekele as well as the regional hubs of Aksum and Shire. 

Three days earlier, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) and six other armed groups had announced a new alliance aimed at overthrowing Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government.

Unexpectedly, the alliance was joined by the Amhara Fano National Movement, which had supported federal forces against the TPLF during the 2020-2022 war, but has since then switched side and turned to fighting the federal government.

The federal government and Tigrayan forces meanwhile have accused each other of starting the latest escalation, both sides portraying their military actions as defensive in nature.

The unraveling of Ethiopia's fragile peace accord

Depending on the source, between 162,000 and 600,000 people were killed in the brutal 2020-2022 war, which was fought over the political status of the northern province of Tigray.

The war ended in November 2022 with the Pretoria Agreement, under which the TPLF agreed to the disarmament, demobilization and reintegration of its combatants, and to respect the federal government's constitutional authority.

However, key provisions remained unimplemented and major disputes unresolved, including the status of contested territories, the return of displaced people and the full demobilization of Tigrayan forces.

Meanwhile, a power struggle within the TPLF ended with the more hardline faction around Debretsion Gebremichael reasserting control in Tigray, further straining relations with Addis Ababa.

The TPLF also reinstated Tigray's pre-war regional council, a move the federal government viewed as a violation of the Pretoria framework.

Concerns mounted even further when the TPLF lost its legal party legislation, thus excluding the party from participating in national elections in June this year.

Tensions steadily increased, culminating in renewed clashes between Tigrayan and federal forces beginning in August 2026.

Fears grow over civilian toll and rights violations

Local residents meanwhile are bracing for further fighting, as organizations like the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) have managed to evacuate only few people caught up in the conflict.

According to the ICRC, the global NGO got to evacuate only around 160 individuals from Tigray, including Ethiopian Federal Police personnel, Ethiopian Airlines staff and African Union monitors.

With reports of damage to civilian infrastructure, disruptions to essential services and interrupted communication and transport routes, observers are worried about the situation of residents not only in Tigray but all across northern Ethiopia.

Amdegebreal Admassu, an Ethiopian lawyer focused on political and legal affairs, told DW he had received reports of fighters impacting public facilities including hospitals, schools and religious institutions.

"We observe instances where these facilities — which also serve as shelters for residents — are either accidentally hit or deliberately targeted.

"Under both international law and our country's penal code, such actions are classified as war crimes," Amdegebreal further explained.

Nearly everyone in Tigray impacted by fighting

Mebrihi Birhane, vice director for the NGO Human Rights First Ethiopia, told DW that many of those civilian facilities had already been impacted during the 2020-22 war.

"The population must have access to essential services even in times of war. Ensuring this is an obligation for all armed forces involved in the conflict," he said.

Meanwhile, the prices of goods are reported to be increasing dramatically, as supply routes are disrupted, affecting residents of Tigray whose communities had so far been spared from the direct fighting.

The latest reports indicate that Tigrayan forces have advanced into the Afar region and were said to be controling the area around Erebti.

Analysts say this advance could be aimed at threatening Ethiopia's main trade corridor — a vital route used for imports and exports and a lifeline for the country's economy.

The renewed conflict meanwhile could spread beyond the confines of Ethiopia to the Horn of Africa and beyond, as Prime Minister Abiy has already accused neighboring countries of picking sides and supporting rebel forces.

Several DW journalists contributed to this report.

Edited by: Sertan Sanderson

entries.title: TV journalist is crowned king of Uganda's Tooro Kingdom
entries.summary: Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma has ascended to the throne after King Oyo died at the age of 34 due to a cancer battle. He previously worked for Ugandan broadcaster UBC as a TV anchor and editor.
entries.content:
Uganda

TV journalist is crowned king of Uganda's Tooro Kingdom

September 29, 2026

Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma has ascended to the throne after King Oyo died at the age of 34 due to a cancer battle. He previously worked for Ugandan broadcaster UBC as a TV anchor and editor.

A TV journalist on Tuesday was crowned king of Uganda's Tooro Kingdom.

What do we know so far?

Edward Rukidi Kiganangoma has ascended to the thrown after his predecessor, King Oyo Kyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, died unexpectedly last month.

King Oyo was only 34 and had lost his cancer battle while receiving treatment in the US. Oyo had became king at only three years of age.   

Oyo's death sparked a succession battle in Uganda, with Oyo's mother pushing for the late king's undisclosed son to be the next monarch.

However, the royal Babito clan chose Kiganangoma, now Nyabongo I, as the heir to the throne out of a group of eligible princes.

Kiganangoma took part in a coronation ceremony in the remote town of Fort Portal in western Uganda to ascend to the throne.

Coronation rituals included a mock battle and animal sacrifices. The ceremony in Fort Portal was televised and attended by thousands of people.

Kiganangoma, who is 56 years old, had worked as a journalist and editor for Ugandan public broadcaster UBC.

Tooro's new king vows to 'protect our culture, our traditions and customs'

"We have a big task to protect our culture, our traditions and customs and good conduct among our people," the new king said in his maiden speech. He had also told the New Vision newspaper: "My family never let me treat royal descent as an entitlement."

Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni was present for the coronation ceremony of the new king. 

While expressing sadness over King Oyo's passing, Museveni also said he congratulates "his Highness Nyabongo. I have been watching him on the news and he is a good newsreader. I am sure he will do a good job."

Uganda is a constitutional republic with a president voted in democratically.

However, the country's four major precolonial kingdoms still hold cultural influence over the East African nation, despite not wielding any political power. The kings are involved in maintaining social order and safeguarding the heritage of their respective kingdoms.

Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko

entries.title: Satirist launches site naming Cornell students accused in gang-rape lawsuit
entries.summary: Writer Toby Morton is using a new website to amplify allegations in a high-profile sexual assault lawsuit involving seven Cornell students. The reopening of the case is causing an outcry on social media.
entries.content:
September 29, 2026

Writer Toby Morton is using a new website to amplify allegations in a high-profile sexual assault lawsuit involving seven Cornell students. The reopening of the case is causing an outcry on social media.

Toby Morton, who wrote several episodes of the animated comedy series "South Park," launched a website seeking accountability in connection with an alleged 2024 sexual assault case involving seven fraternity members at Cornell University in the US. The site names seven men accused of sexually assaulting a 20-year-old woman who was allegedly unconscious after being given drugs and alcohol at a Cornell fraternity house, and collects personal data and photos of the members involved.

"I've received messages reminding me I'm not a journalist, I'm 'just a satirist,'" Morton wrote in a September 27 Instagram post regarding the creation of his website TheCornell7.org. "This is true, but it makes me more dangerous," he added, saying he has "nobody to tell me I've gone too far."

The case has recently drawn a surge in public attention after the accuser, identified as Jane Doe to protect her identity, filed a lawsuit in mid-September. Her complaint alleges that she was brutally sexually assaulted in 2024 by seven members of the Chi Phi fraternity while unconscious after being pressured to take ketamine, smoke marijuana and drink alcohol at the fraternity house on Cornell's campus in Ithaca, New York. The university, she said in the lawsuit, failed to protect her. Cornell conducted an internal investigation after the incident, but no one was charged.

Since the lawsuit was filed on September 16, the case has generated widespread commentary on social media. Some have criticized Cornell and the district attorney's office, while others have questioned the allegations.

Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten, who handled the original case, said his office has reopened it and plans to present evidence to a grand jury amid public questions about why no criminal charges were initially filed.

Van Houten said in a statement that his office is considering bringing criminal charges related to the incident, though the allegations in the civil complaint are "dramatically different" from the woman's statement to police two years ago — in her statement to authorities, she did not allege she was drugged without her knowledge or that she did not consent to engage in sexual acts.

Justice sought

Cornell's Chi Phi chapter was barred from campus after the alleged incident in 2024. The woman who accused the men of sexual assault dropped out of Cornell University, according to her attorney. 

One of the most chilling allegations of the lawsuit is that a message was sent to a Chi Phi Snapchat group at about 1:42 a.m., inviting members to the room to abuse Doe, who was heavily under the influence of drugs and alcohol. The lawsuit alleges that more men then entered the room and that the assault continued for several hours until Doe lost consciousness.

"There were so many people that could have prevented it and they didn't. I've never seen anything like it," an attorney for Jane Doe, Thomas Giuffra, told CBS.

Giuffra pointed out that two of the seven accused fraternity members were expelled, while the others received lesser disciplinary measures.

"Not one of these guys was arrested," Giuffra told the network.

Politicians and actors speak out

Many people, from US politicians to Hollywood actors, have spoken out about the case in recent days. US Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, a New York Democrat, condemned what she described as a "culture of rape" protected by elite institutions.

"When I read what happened at Cornell, those men posted in a group chat. That means it was normal to them. That means it was acceptable to them. This is a culture, and what we must do is understand that we cannot protect those spaces anymore," she said Sunday at a forum near Cornell's campus.

British actress Florence Pugh described the allegations as "horrific" on social media and expressed her support for the student involved.

Pugh, who is currently on a promotional tour for her upcoming Netflix series "East of Eden," wrote a lengthy statement on Instagram, saying that "Colleges/schools/universities repeatedly fail women around the world. You build men that get taught through time and time again that they can do extreme harm and that they won't be harmed in return."

"Those who protect and impose light sentences on men who rape and destroy lives should be punished and closely scrutinized. Why are you protecting someone so fiercely?" she wrote.

American actor Josh Gad, best known as the voice of Olaf in Disney's"Frozen" films, also commented on the Cornell case, criticizing what he described as insufficient disciplinary consequences for the students accused of sexual assault. In an Instagram post, Gad said sexual violence should not be treated as a mistake or addressed with limited disciplinary action by a university. 

He argued that the alleged conduct had "destroyed a life" and called for greater accountability.



Edited by Joshua Lang.

entries.title: Senegal's Youth Olympics makes Olympics in Africa 'logical'
entries.summary: The Youth Olympics are to be hosted in Africa for the first time ever. The edition in Senegal is also a chance to prove the continent can host a full Olympics in the future.
entries.content:
September 29, 2026

The Youth Olympics are to be hosted in Africa for the first time ever. The edition in Senegal is also a chance to prove the continent can host a full Olympics in the future.

At the end of October 2026, the first ever Olympic event on African soil will take place as the Youth Olympics comes to Senegal.

Around 2,700 young athletes are expected to compete across a total of 153 events in 25 sports, with many qualifying through the African Youth Games last year.

"We were entrusted with hosting this event and that is why from Johannesburg to Nairobi, from Dakar to Djbouti, it is all of young Africa that is watching you and watching you with pride," Senegalese President Bassirou Diomaye Faye said at the arrival of the flame.

The moment marks yet another step forward for global sport in Africa. In 2025, the first major road cycling event took place on the continent, and in September this year it was announced the first-ever World Athletics Championships would be held in Kenya in 2029. There are also on-going negotiations about Formula 1 returning. It appears that 16 years on since the 2010 World Cup in South Africa, global sport is finally returning to different parts of Africa.

"This is a victory for Africa. It opens the door for Africa to host major events," Malick Diouf, head of a marketing agency and founder of the Dakar Sport Summit, told DW.

"Africa is in the process of opening up to the world, hosting major events and everything. And all of Africa must celebrate this kind of victory."

With more major events in Africa, the question around an Olympic Games being on the continent looms.

Sports scientist Kamilla Swart has said awarding Africa a Games would make the world "take Africa more seriously." Diouf believes it's the logical next step.

"The Youth Olympic Games, it's a major test for Africa. And I think this is where we need to succeed in organizing these Games and also in sending a message," Diouf said.

"We, Africa, are ready to host the Summer Olympics, and I think that would be the logical next step after the Dakar Olympics. We have Olympic champions; we have record holders; we have Olympians, so we deserve to host the Olympic Games."

Senegal an attractive option for many reasons

The move to re-use and refurbish existing facilities rather than build whole new ones is likely why Senegal's bid was so tempting for the International Olympic Committee (IOC).

The fear of the white elephant facility appears to have been considered here. The Iba Mar Diop Stadium, the track and field stadium, is expected to be used for athlete training ahead of the 2028 Olympics.

"It’s by using these facilities, by participating in and hosting international events, and by consistently maintaining them to the required standards, that we’ll be able to keep these stadiums up to the standards they currently meet," Diouf said.

There's also the social and economical impacts of the Youth Olympics. Diouf believes the impact is beyond just infrastructure, but into roads, the development of the hospitality, security and broadcasting sectors and the young athletes themselves.

"There's life after the Games. Now we need to figure out how to use the resources we have, we need to develop and capitalize on what we have showcased during the Games," said Diouf.

Future of Youth Olympics in doubt

The significance of these Games stretch beyond even the history they are making in Africa. In May of this year, IOC President Kirsty Coventry put the brakes on the future of the Youth Olympics, leaving real doubts as to whether there will be any more after the 2028 winter edition.

"We need to pause and have a real reflection on why we're doing the Youth Olympic Games and we realized that across the Movement it's very disjointed. There's not a true North Star of why we're doing the Youth Olympic Games," Coventry told reporters.

"So the EB (IOC Executive Board) decided to pause the 2030 process right now so there will not be an election in June, and rather we need to take a step back and develop a youth strategy."

A lot has changed since the Youth Olympic Games were launched in 2010. Initially it was seen as a way to engage a younger audience (athletes were limited by age to between 15 and 18) by trialing new sports as well as testing host country's on a smaller stage. However, with the age of athletes decreasing and the challenges of engaging a younger audience in the modern sports entertainment landscape even more challenging, it appears clear the IOC are reconsidering their options when it comes to investment.

"My only wish is that Dakar be memorable and that people reconsider their decision not to host the Games in 2030," Diouf said.

"I don’t want these to be the last Youth Olympic Games, but if these are to be the last Youth Olympic Games, we need to go out with a bang. Dakar needs to show the world what Senegal is all about, what Africa is all about."

From October 31 to November 13 this year, Senegal will have the chance to do just that.

Edited by: Chuck Penfold

entries.title: UK PM Burnham seeks 'hope again' at Labour Party conference
entries.summary: Andy Burnham is seeking a delicate balance between optimism and realism at Labour's annual party conference. He promised hope and an end to "politics as usual" but also an "honest conversation" about difficult dilemmas.
entries.content:
United Kingdom

UK PM Burnham seeks 'hope again' at Labour Party conference

September 29, 2026

Andy Burnham is seeking a delicate balance between optimism and realism at Labour's annual party conference. He promised hope and an end to "politics as usual" but also an "honest conversation" about difficult dilemmas.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, only in the role for a few months after replacing Keir Starmer, has told the Labour Party conference in his native Liverpool that his government wants to restore hope and end "politics as usual." 

But the UK's seventh prime minister in a decade is trying to balance a series of evidently conflicting fiscal goals: bolstering economic growth, reducing cost-of-living pressures, safeguarding pensions and making care costs more affordable, upgrading creaking infrastructure and significantly boosting military spending.

That's all while battling a populist challenge from Reform UK and Restore Britain on the right and the Green Party on the left. This led Labour to severe local and regional election defeats in May and ultimately spelt his predecessor Starmer's demise. 

What did Burnham say in his conference speech?

Burnham, a Liverpool lad who was mayor of Manchester prior to moving to take up Britain's top political job, repeated his most common mantra since coming to power, namely that "more of the same" will not solve the various issues facing the UK.

"We can't carry on as we are. Politics as usual has taken Britain backwards," Burnham said. "More of the same isn't good enough and isn't going to get us where we need to be."

The conference's banner headline "hope again" was not incompatible with a more honest conversation, Burnham said.

"Hope comes from honesty ... and saying the things politicians usually avoid," he said.

He cited Labour's post-war government under Clement Atlee, famed for achievements like setting up Britain's National Health Service, as an example of his party's past credentials, having "built the peace" in the public interest. He said that since the 1980s and the Conservative-dominated Margaret Thatcher era of his youth, this direction was lost.

"I will say it straight, Britain has been on the wrong path for a long time. Deindustrialization, deregulation, privatization, austerity, Brexit, and what has it given us? A country run for vested interests, not in the public interest — with power held in too few hands, and too many places left to drift," Burnham said.

Burnham told the audience he would take on "the difficult issues that have been ignored for too long," including social care, high levels of youth unemployment, and greater public control of once-nationalized core interests like energy, water and housing.

"The British right talk about 'taking back control," Burnham said, evoking the slogan of the 2016 Brexit campaign. "Never forget that they are the ones who gave it away in the first place!"

Why is Burnham, and Britain, in such a tricky bind?

Burnham said on coming to power that he wanted his premiership to be a "circuit-breaker for Britain" after years of rising prices and anemic growth.

He hit the ground with a handful of new policies like a cap on bus fares, temporarily removing value added tax from electricity bills amid the Iran war, and announcing a bid to stamp out rough sleeping.

But critics say his more grand stated strategy lacks detail and could prove economically unfeasible.

Burnham is constrained by a series of factors, including Labour's 2024 election campaign pledges under Starmer's leadership, Britain's strained public finances, and the suddenly risk-averse debt markets that have started heaping pressure on most developed economies of late.

Borrowing costs for his UK government, as it eyes a series of new banner spending plans, hit a 10-year-high on the morning of Burnham's speech.

Pledges for a 'National Care System' and commission on electoral reform

In a sign of this lacking spending wiggle room, Burnham has already pushed back his stated aim to formulate reform plans for Britain's social care system.

He said on Tuesday that a "National Care System" would be put forward in time for the next election, currently scheduled for 2029. He said it would be a change "as significant" to the UK as the foundation of the state-funded National Health Service, and also essential to ensure the wider NHS' survival.

He said the plan would be "fully funded, and not by borrowing."

Burnham said that he did not expect such reforms to be easy, and acknowledged "I may pay a political price," but he said they were necessary steps and the kind of leadership he'd promised the party when seeking to replace Starmer this summer. 

These challenging economic realities coincide with Labour facing multi-pronged political threats. They hail from right-wing populist parties like the anti-immigration Reform UK, from left-wing populists claiming to hold an economic magic wand like the Green Party, and from nationalist parties in Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland advocating independence from the UK.

Burnham also issued appeal to rival political parties late in his speech, saying he would seek as much cross-party consensus as possible for his plans.

He also announced that he would set up a "new national commission on electoral reform," inviting all other parties to contribute to its work.

He said Labour would stand in 2029's election on a platform of reforming the UK voting system so that "every person's vote counts," as party members had advocated in repeated conference votes in past years.

For decades, successive Labour and Conservative governments would not touch Britain's winner-takes-all first-past-the-post voting system, because they were major beneficiaries of it.

What do people say about Burnham's message?

The sense in Liverpool is that Burnham is getting through with his message. Paul James is a taxi driver and union member from Manchester, who says that he has met Burnham while he was Manchester's mayor and that he trusts him: "He never says he can do something unless he can do it." He wants the new prime minister to focus on building council houses, as Burnham is promising once more in his speech he would do.

Pollster Luke Tryl summarizes what Burnham does well: "People think he gets them," he understands their concerns.

Stephen Kinsella from the pressure goup Patriotic Millionnaires hopes that Burnham will focus on wealth taxes. And while there is no concrete plan for higher taxes for richer people, it is clear that Burnham's ambitious plans, like "fixing the broken social care" system, will require extra funds.

"He communicates a sense of optimism, a sense that we can do things as a country," he added.

Kinsella also hopes that Burnham will edge Britain closer to Europe — a sentiment that was echoed at some of the fringe meetings.

Ann Webster, a headteacher from Leicester, is talking passionately about conversations she has had with her Brexit-voting community at home: "People are not stupid, they have noticed that they are poorer after Brexit."

And indeed, Burnham acknowledged in his speech that "Brexit has not given us control — Brexit has done more harm than good."

He promised to build consensus around a new relationship with Europe, without going into details.

entries.title: North Korea has recently completed two road bridges easing transport to strategic allies Russia and China
entries.summary: Two recently opened bridges are expected to ease trade and transport between North Korea and its powerful neighbors. The new connections come as Pyongyang builds strategic ties with China and Russia.
entries.content:
September 29, 2026

Two recently opened bridges are expected to ease trade and transport between North Korea and its powerful neighbors. The new connections come as Pyongyang builds strategic ties with China and Russia.

A long-delayed bridge linking North Korea and China could finally open in early October, more than a decade after its completion, as Pyongyang simultaneously expands transport links with Russia.

South Korean news outlets have reported that the New Yalu River Bridge, connecting China's northeastern city of Dandong with the trade hub of Sinuiju in northwestern North Korea, could formally open by October 6, which marks the 77th anniversary of North Korea-China diplomatic relations.

Analysis published by the 38 North think tank showed significant progress on customs, immigration and warehouse facilities on the North Korean side, where construction had remained largely unfinished for years.

The cable-stayed New Yalu River Bridge is located about 15 kilometers (9 miles) downstream toward the Yellow Sea from the older crossings connecting central Dandong and Sinuiju.

The four-lane road bridge stretches over 3,000 meters across the river, with a network of approach roads connecting it to the surrounding areas.

It was intended to ease pressure on the aging Sino-Korean Friendship Bridge, which carries both road and rail traffic and remains one of the most important routes between North Korea and China, Pyongyang's top trading partner.

Improving links to both Russia and China

The expected opening of the improved link with China comes after a road bridge crossing the Tumen River located across the peninsula was opened on September 7 connecting North Korea's Rason region with Khasan in Russia's Primorsky region.

Until then, the two countries' narrow land border had been connected by rail but not by road.

"North Korea allowed the Chinese bridge to sit unused for more than a decade, but North Korea hurried more than Russia did," Han Ki-bum, a former deputy director of South Korea's National Intelligence Service, told DW.

That difference, he argues, provides clues to Pyongyang's strategy, which appears to be deliberately managing the pace of its improving relations with Russia and China to avoid returning to excessive dependence on Beijing.

"If it depends too much on China as it did in the past, North Korea's autonomy could be undermined," Han said, adding that Pyongyang is seeking to take advantage of good ties with both China and Russia while preserving its independence.

The former Unification Ministry official added that Russia has an interest in expanding transport routes through North Korea toward the Pacific, including through the port of Rajin, while Pyongyang could benefit from increased trade, tourism and opportunities to send workers to Russia.

He added that Russia needs North Korean labor, arguing that North Korean workers are more diligent than their Russian counterparts.

China, meanwhile, has its own reasons to ensure that North Korea does not become excessively reliant on Russia, the former official said.

"From China's perspective, it needs to keep North Korea from leaning too far toward Russia," Han said.

Ties between Moscow and Pyongyang have grown since 2023, when North Korea began providing weapons and troops for the Ukraine war. As the Russia-North Korea strategic relationship has deepened, China has been taking steps to reassert itself as the North's primary partner.

Ahn Chan-il, a former North Korean soldier who now heads the World Institute for North Korea Studies in Seoul, said the bridges have added geopolitical implications.

"Pyongyang could now use its deepening ties with China and Russia, along with Trump's interest in engaging Kim, to strengthen its diplomatic leverage and take a more assertive approach toward South Korea," Ahn told DW. 

North Korea slowly reopens

Pyongyang virtually sealed its borders during the COVID-19 pandemic, sharply reducing trade and restricting even the entry of foreign diplomats.

Cross-border freight trains between Dandong and Sinuiju resumed in 2022. Passenger trains followed on March 12 this year, restoring rail travel between North Korea and China for the first time in six years.

Ahn described the prospective bridge opening as historically significant.

"The New Yalu River Bridge is effectively the first modern bridge between North Korea and China," Ahn said.

Plans for a new bridge date to 2009, when then-Chinese Premier Wen Jiabao and North Korean officialsagreed on the project to relieve the Sino-Korean Friendship Bridge, built in 1943.

Construction on the new bridge began in 2011, largely financed by Beijing, and the bridge itself was essentially completed in 2014. The opening was complicated by delays on building a customs center on the North Korean side.

Ahn added the opening could be interpreted as a signal that Pyongyang intends to move toward greater economic openness, even if that process proceeds slowly.

Yalu River Bridge to bolster China trade

A former senior South Korean Unification Ministry official, who requested anonymity, told DW that renewed trade could also benefit China's northeastern provinces of Liaoning, Jilin and Heilongjiang.

Before sanctions and the pandemic disrupted commerce, businesses in the region imported North Korean goods, including seafood, while Chinese products flowed in the opposite direction.

"Both sides need this," the former official said.

North Korea needs Chinese goods and opportunities to earn foreign currency, while parts of northeastern China can benefit from renewed cross-border commerce, he added.

The official said the long delay also reflected Pyongyang's previous reluctance to build customs, logistics and other infrastructure required on its side.

"The fact that it is opening now means North Korea has built customs, clearance facilities and logistics warehouses," he said. "From that perspective, North Korea needs it more. It now needs goods coming in from China."

Former South Korean intelligence official Han expects the new crossing to accelerate trade recovery toward pre-pandemic trade levels.

"The opening of the Yalu River bridge will further stimulate trade between North Korea and China," Han told DW.

North Korea particularly needs imports for construction and industrial production, including factory components, he said.

But Han cautioned against expecting an uncontrolled trade boom.

He pointed to Pyongyang's increasingly centralized trade system, under which the state has tightened control over imports instead of allowing individual factories and enterprises to conduct commerce more independently.

A shortage of foreign currency could provide another constraint, Han said, pointing to the sharp rise in the unofficial exchange rate for the US dollar inside North Korea.

Edited by: Wesley Rahn
